name: Fern Green
lede: Fern Green is a mid, slightly dulled green, dated by Maerz and Paul to 1902 and later adopted by RAL and Crayola.

sections.title: One green, several lists
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, by the account the NBS carried into its 1955 circular, puts the first printed record of the name at 1902, on plate 21 F 5 [1]. The German RAL system later listed its own approximate match in 1927 as RAL 6025, and Wikipedia's Crayola-sourced entry and the 2010 xkcd color survey both cite the same green [1]. The ISCC-NBS system reads it as a strong green, about 9.9 units from the block center, a looser match than most [1].

The nearest named color in our data is [[velvet-green]], about 5.4 units off, with [[dark-sage]] and [[forest-green]] further out [2]. The family word is [[fern]] itself [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This color, as photographed, appears in 99 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.42 percent, more common than 50 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 14 of 1,674 paintings, at 0.8 percent of that period's paintings, 3.5 times the overall rate [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent [3]. It is most over-represented in France (3.1 times expected; 29 of 3443 paintings) [3]. The earliest match in the archive is a 1500 painting by Pedro Berruguete, 427 years before the name's 1927 record, so this is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a pigment identification, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3].

issues: Fixed: the field-notes paragraph (and the matching "field" object) invented four painter names ("Van Gogh, Pissarro, Munch and Gauguin") with no basis — ar.pa/ar.pn are empty for this slug (the real over-representation is a country, France, 29 of 3,443, 3.1x, which went unmentioned) — and an earliest-match painter ("Lucas Cranach the Elder") and record year (1902) that don't match the real data (first-seen is a 1500 painting by Pedro Berruguete; the real record year is 1927). The presence count (70) and peak-decade stat (1910s/1.9%/6x+) also didn't match the real data (99 as-photographed; peak is the 1900s century fact, 0.8%/3.5x). Rewrote the paragraph directly from data/graph/fieldnotes for this slug; removed every unsupported claim rather than inventing a replacement for it.
